design.hypothesis: After the receiver-lock change, small-file fresh copies are limited by per-file work on the receiving Mac. If so, -j8 and -j16 give little over -j4 while peer CPU rises, and the effect is stronger on pull (mars>mac), where small-deep takes about twice as long as push. --no-atomic at -j8 beats -j8 if temp-file rename costs matter. A large gap between durable_s and wall_s would point at writeback. This run leaves out the local tar-extraction baseline on the receiver and any sample/perf profile, so it bounds the limit by scaling and CPU, not by an absolute ceiling or a per-function breakdown.

trees.question: What limits xs's small-file fresh copies once the receiver's global lock and serial final pass are gone, and what removes the next limit?

nodes.title: Race the receiver-lock branch
nodes.result: fresh 0.411 (faster) / noop 1.007 (inconclusive). The receiver-lock branch (c5b765eb54fc against b02ae2394a86) is clearly faster on fresh copies: 'fresh 0.411 (faster)' with a 95% interval of 0.406 to 0.415 over 8 blocks. That is the minimum block count, but the interval is narrow and far below 1. No-op re-syncs are unchanged within noise: 'noop 1.007 (inconclusive)', interval 0.962 to 1.055. Keep it and merge. The pooled verdicts do not separate the default, --no-atomic and -j8 configurations, so whether extra receiving workers now help is not answered by these facts; A2 should look at that split.

trees.question: Where does a re-sync that changes nothing spend its time, and can it skip unchanged subtrees?

nodes.title: Re-measure no-op syncs
nodes.result: no verdict. The run's status is 'failed' and it carries no lab verdicts, so this branch rests on the arm-vs-control effects alone. Some cells kept only 8 or 9 of 10 blocks. Even so, the hypothesis that xs-rs still trails rsync on no-op re-syncs is refuted. At the default -j4, xs-rs against rsync was 0.269 (0.235 to 0.309, 10 blocks) on congress push and 0.308 (0.262 to 0.361, 10 blocks) on congress pull. It was 0.231 (0.219 to 0.245, 8 blocks) on psample push. The one weak cell is psample pull at -j4: 0.6 with a 95% interval of 0.213 to 1.689 over 9 blocks, too wide to call, at 45.418 s against 75.716 s. At -j8 xs-rs is clearly ahead in all four cells: 0.249, 0.268, 0.185, and 0.191 (0.147 to 0.249) on psample pull. -j1 is also ahead everywhere it is decided: 0.519, 0.584 and 0.421, with psample pull at 0.82 (0.317 to 2.121), inconclusive. Going from -j1 to -j8 roughly halves time on every cell, so no serial bottleneck dominates. xs-rs CPU seconds are close to rsync's at -j4 (7.747 vs 8.098 on congress push), not far above. The lab records only total CPU, not a user/kernel split, so branches 0 and 1 could not be told apart anyway, and neither is needed: xs-rs is at or ahead of rsync both ways. The remaining oddity is the high variance of psample pull at -j4 (and xs-cpp-j4 there at 2.002, 0.912 to 4.393). That is noise worth watching, not a deficit against rsync. A measurement changes no code, so keep is false.

nodes.title: Compression for slow links
nodes.result: fresh 1.001 (equivalent) / noop 0.991 (inconclusive). The compression change (c9e8d5d5f87d against 0a4953bec5d8) did not make copies faster on this link. Fresh copies were 'fresh 1.001 (equivalent)', 95% interval 0.974 to 1.030 over 8 blocks, at 12.42 s against 12.402 s. No-op re-syncs were 'noop 0.991 (inconclusive)', interval 0.942 to 1.043 over 8 blocks, at 1.714 s against 1.73 s. Eight blocks is the minimum. The fresh interval is reasonably tight around 1, but the no-op interval is wide, so this is weak evidence in both directions. The race also ran on mac-mars-usb10g, not on lab2's internet link, so it says nothing for or against the 'faster on lab2' branch. On the 10 GbE cable, where negative levels were meant to help, it bought no time. No later node depends on it. Drop it from the chain; the dictionary and long-range ideas would need a separate slow-link race.
